message.content: {"distractor_2":"Use a single persistent client connection with per-server logical sessions: namespaced messages, separate capability records, and isolated tokens managed by the host.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_2":"Incorrect: logical namespacing still fails to provide true server-side session semantics. Servers expect per-connection initialization, subscription registries, and connection-bound credentials. Emulating sessions inside one connection can break capability negotiation order, subscription lifecycles, notification routing, and server-enforced lifecycle or authentication assumptions, risking misrouting and consent or capability leaks.","thinking_process_2":"Chose a plausible alternative that virtualizes sessions within one connection (namespacing, per-server state). Ensured the mistake differs from prior proxy/multiplexing error by focusing on inability to replicate server-side session semantics, lifecycle, and connection-bound auth rather than on transport-level multiplexing. Counted words to meet the 22–24 requirement."}

{"distractor_2":"Keep the server connection open, insert a host-side redaction proxy to strip sensitive tokens and send only sanitized context, monitor activity and review access logs.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_2":"Incorrect because it leaves a potentially compromised connection active and relies on after-the-fact redaction and logging; prior exposure and credential compromise require termination, audit, and credential rotation to restore host-enforced isolation and preserve authoritative local history.","thinking_process_2":"Core concept: servers must not read the whole conversation and full history stays with the host. I produced a plausible mitigation—host-side redaction and monitoring—that would reduce data sent going forward. This is wrong here because it fails to terminate the compromised connection, rotate credentials, or guarantee the host retains authoritative, isolated history; those steps are required by the protocol."}

{"distractor_2":"Require cryptographically signed UI packages, enforce host integrity checks, permit direct DOM embedding for performance, and rely on user warnings.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_2":"Signatures attest origin but don't guarantee safe behavior; embedding UI into the host DOM removes sandboxing and prevents auditable JSON-RPC and explicit consent, breaking defense-in-depth.","thinking_process_2":"I picked a plausible security-by-signature plus performance tradeoff approach that might work elsewhere. It seems attractive because signed bundles and integrity checks feel authoritative and direct DOM embedding reduces latency. However, this conflicts with the MCP proposal's layered defenses: signatures don't replace predeclared host review, iframe sandboxing, auditable message routing, explicit user consent, or text-only fallbacks, so it leaves hosts vulnerable to runtime or behavioral risks."}

{"distractor_2":"Derive a deterministic ID by hashing request payload client-side, reusing identical-request hashes across retries and sessions for simplicity.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_2":"Incorrect because identical payloads produce the same non-null ID, causing reused IDs within a session and violating per-requestor uniqueness.","thinking_process_2":"Picked deterministic hashing as a plausible idempotency/deduplication strategy; it's attractive for retries but wrongly allows repeated identical IDs within the same requestor session, breaking the MCP requirement that IDs must not have been previously used by that requestor."}

{"distractor_2":"Require all implementations to implement base protocol, lifecycle management, server features, client features, and utilities as mandatory for full interoperability across vendors","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_2":"Wrong because the MCP explicitly requires only the base protocol and lifecycle management as MUST; server features, client features, and utilities are optional (MAY).","thinking_process_2":"Chose a plausible stricter policy—making every component mandatory—to mirror the correct answer's tone. This is believable for ensuring uniform capabilities but conflicts with the spec's modular, optional components and so is incorrect for this protocol."}

{"distractor_2":"Execute tools entirely in-browser via WebAssembly, let clients perform model selection locally, rely on client-side logging and browser storage for auditing and execution.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_2":"Browser-based execution can't access protected backend data or hardened hosts, so it cannot act as the auditable execution/logging boundary or follow MCP's client-invoked server tool flow.","thinking_process_2":"I created a plausible low-latency alternative (running tools in the browser) that fits some decentralised designs but fails here because MCP assumes clients invoke managed MCP servers with access to sensitive data and observable logs; browsers cannot securely provide that execution boundary, discovery, or transport-aware health checks."}

{"distractor_2":"Use shared user-level OAuth2 access and refresh tokens with broad offline_access scopes, a single consent screen, centralized audit logs, and token rotation.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_2":"Wrong because sharing user-level OAuth tokens and relying on broad offline_access plus a single consent prevents per-agent scoping, fine-grained consent, immediate per-agent revocation, and per-action attribution required by MCP.","thinking_process_2":"I chose a familiar OAuth2 pattern that looks operationally simple—shared access/refresh tokens, single consent, and rotation—but realized MCP demands distinct per-agent short-lived tokens, explicit per-agent consent screens, revocation APIs, and per-action audit logs to enforce least-privilege and enable narrow revocation and attribution, so this approach is unsuitable."}

{"distractor_2":"On server: rely on mutual TLS authentication and signed requests, sandbox tools, and stream raw outputs; on client: show inputs, cache results, and perform minimal validation.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_2":"Wrong because transport-level authentication and sandboxing are insufficient under MCP: servers still MUST validate inputs, enforce access controls, rate-limit, and sanitize outputs; streaming raw outputs breaks sanitization requirements.","thinking_process_2":"Created a plausible alternate focused on transport security and sandboxing (different from cloud IAM offload). Kept the same two-part server/client phrasing, made it technically credible but wrong because MCP mandates explicit server-side validation, access control, rate limiting, and output sanitization. Counted words to ensure the distractor is 26 words."}

{"distractor_2":"Move destructive operations behind an admin-only service, enforce RBAC and CI code review, use feature flags, manual approvals, audit trails, rollbackable releases","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_2":"This is wrong because it shifts safety to deployment/ops rather than providing tool-level runtime safeguards. It omits explicit side-effect annotations, per-call human confirmations, idempotent job IDs, progress/status reporting, parameter JSON validation, enforced timeouts, rate limiting, and focused atomic operations required by the MCP guidance.","thinking_process_2":"I selected a plausible governance-first solution (admin service, RBAC, CI reviews, feature flags) that organizations often use. It appears safe but fails here because the MCP guidance requires runtime, tool-level controls (annotations, confirmations, idempotency, progress, timeouts, rate limits, schema validation, and logs) rather than only deployment-time protections."}

{"distractor_2":"Build a thin compatibility shim that implements only a minimal MCP subset, mapping LLM calls to internal APIs and avoiding full protocol compliance.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_2":"This is wrong because implementing only a subset risks incompatibility with other MCP-compliant services; it undermines interoperability guarantees and increases long-term maintenance and integration drift.","thinking_process_2":"I proposed a pragmatic shortcut to reduce immediate engineering effort by mapping only needed features to internal APIs. While plausible for fast delivery, it conflicts with the source’s emphasis on using a shared, open specification to ensure consistent behavior, validation, and cross-vendor interoperability, so it would create fragile, nonstandard integrations."}

{"distractor_2":"Option C: Return remote-DOM or JSON UI descriptors instructing host to render native widgets or modify the host DOM.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_2":"Wrong because the initial MCP Apps spec only accepts self-contained text/html in sandboxed iframes; remote DOM or widget instructions require host DOM access and are explicitly deferred, breaking the sandboxed rendering model and consistent previews.","thinking_process_2":"I picked remote-DOM/JSON descriptors because they enable lightweight, declarative UIs and native integration, but they conflict with the spec\u0002s requirement for sandboxed text/html and the deferral of remote DOM/native widgets."}
